error_modes.label: Knowledge of the exercises given as daily assignment for the navigation sortie

texts.0: SP, due to lack of knowledge of the published procedure for the condition encountered, could not state the legs, the turning points or the completion criteria of the exercises given as daily assignment for the navigation sortie. SP did not know in detail all exercises given as daily assignment, so the IP had to present the whole route and the associated exercises from the beginning at the pre-flight briefing. Two assigned exercises had to be demonstrated in flight before SP could attempt them and the planned navigation legs were not completed as briefed.
texts.1: SP, due to a superficial review of the daily assignment, recalled the navigation exercises only in outline and produced the planned headings, times and altitudes only after repeated verbal prompting by the IP. Knowledge of the assigned exercises stayed at the minimum acceptable limit and the sequence of legs had to be restated verbally before each turning point. SP flew the complete route, but the delay in recall left no time for the last assigned exercise.
texts.2: SP, due to studying the daily assignment late in the preparation, hesitated on the entry parameters of two exercises of the navigation profile at the pre-flight briefing. SP identified the gap without IP input, returned to the assignment sheet and restated the correct sequence of legs and the completion criteria before the walk-around. The route was then flown as planned and no exercise had to be re-briefed in flight.
texts.3: SP knew in detail all exercises given as daily assignment and stated the sequence of legs, the planned parameters and the completion criteria of each one without hesitation. Answers at the pre-flight briefing were prompt and accurate and the same knowledge was applied over the route without prompting. The post-flight briefing confirmed correct understanding of every assigned exercise.
texts.4: SP knew every exercise of the daily navigation assignment in exceptional detail, including the reason behind each planned parameter and the errors most commonly associated with it. SP briefed the complete route and the associated exercises to the IP without notes and correctly linked each one to the preceding navigation sorties of the syllabus. Every question at the post-flight briefing was answered accurately and with the correct reference.
texts.marginal: SP knew all exercises given as daily assignment to the required standard, but answers on the later legs of the route were slower and less detailed than on the first ones. The trend indicates that preparation is concentrated on the initial part of the assignment. SP is expected to study the whole assignment with the same depth so that recall is uniform over the complete navigation profile.

texts_at.0: With the IP presenting the route and the associated exercises of the daily assignment at the briefing table, SP followed the sequence read back and needed one exercise demonstrated in flight before it could be attempted. Stating the legs, turning points and completion criteria of the daily assignment without a reminder has not yet been asked of SP independently. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to state one exercise unprompted before doing so for the whole assignment.
texts_at.1: SP recalled the daily assignment inside the standard required at this stage, planned headings, times and altitudes produced only after repeated verbal prompting at the pre-flight briefing. The trend traces to the assignment being reviewed in outline rather than studied to the level of individual leg parameters. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to study to the level of individual leg parameters so recall does not need prompting.
texts_at.2: SP recalled the daily assignment inside the standard required at this stage, hesitating on the entry parameters of two exercises at the briefing before the gap was identified. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to review every exercise's entry parameters, not only the sequence of legs, so hesitation does not appear at the briefing.
texts_at.3: SP knew in detail all exercises given as daily assignment and stated the sequence of legs, the planned parameters and the completion criteria of each one without hesitation, answers at the pre-flight briefing prompt and accurate, the small margin tracing to one answer on the route being a beat slower than the rest. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to hold the same recall speed on every leg so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.1: SP recalled the daily assignment for the sortie, one exercise demonstrated after a verbal reminder from the IP and the rest recalled unprompted. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP identified the gap in the entry parameters of two exercises without IP input, returned to the assignment sheet and restated the correct sequence of legs and completion criteria before the walk-around, after hesitating at the briefing. Reviewing every exercise's entry parameters before the briefing, rather than identifying the gap during it, would remove even that hesitation. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good daily assignment knowledge.
texts_above.3: SP knew in detail all exercises given as daily assignment and stated the sequence of legs, the planned parameters and the completion criteria of each one without hesitation, the same knowledge applied over the route without prompting and confirmed correct at the post-flight briefing. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to very good daily assignment knowledge.
texts_above.4: SP knew every exercise of the daily navigation assignment in exceptional detail, including the reason behind each planned parameter and the errors most commonly associated with it, briefing the complete route to the IP without notes. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to excellent daily assignment knowledge.

error_modes.label: Flight Manual, A/C Techniques and Procedures Manual, AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and aeronautical publications (MAIP, maps)

texts.0: SP, due to not having reviewed the Flight Manual and the A/C Techniques and Procedures Manual before the navigation sortie, quoted an operating limit incorrectly and could not locate the applicable paragraph when asked. SP did not know in detail the publications required for the flight, including AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the aeronautical publications (MAIP, maps), and could not find the route data on the chart. The IP had to state the correct limits, read the procedure aloud and identify the chart entries before the sortie could be briefed.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete study of the Flight Manual and the A/C Techniques and Procedures Manual, produced the correct limit only after the IP indicated the chapter to be opened, and located the MAIP entry for the en-route airfield only after being told where to look. Knowledge of the required publications remained at the minimum acceptable limit and every reference had to be confirmed verbally by the IP. SP finally quoted the correct paragraph and chart data, but the search delayed the pre-flight briefing.
texts.2: SP, due to relying on memory instead of the current publication, misstated one value of the Flight Manual limits at the pre-flight briefing of the navigation sortie. SP recognized the error without IP intervention, opened the manual and gave the correct value together with its paragraph within a few seconds. The remaining questions on the A/C Techniques and Procedures Manual, AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the aeronautical publications (MAIP, maps) were answered accurately.
texts.3: SP knew in detail the Flight Manual, the A/C Techniques and Procedures Manual, AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the aeronautical publications (MAIP, maps) and used them with confidence throughout the navigation sortie. Limits, normal procedures, the applicable VFR rules and the route and airfield data were quoted correctly and with the right reference at both briefings. No answer required correction by the IP.
texts.4: SP used all handbooks related to the flight with complete confidence, quoting limits and procedures verbatim together with chapter and paragraph, and reading the route directly from the current chart and MAIP entries. SP also explained how the Flight Manual limits and the AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 rules applied to the specific route and conditions of the sortie and cross-checked the information between the publications. Knowledge exceeded the level expected at this stage of the syllabus.
texts.marginal: SP knew the Flight Manual and the A/C Techniques and Procedures Manual to the required standard, but answers drawn from AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the aeronautical publications (MAIP, maps) were noticeably slower and more general. The trend shows that study is concentrated on the aircraft handbooks and not on the regulatory and navigation publications, which carry most of the information used on this category. SP is expected to study all handbooks required by BD 3-1/HATC with the same depth so that every reference is used with equal confidence.

texts_at.0: With the IP reading the applicable limit and identifying the chart entries needed for the sortie, SP followed the reference read back and needed two entries identified before the briefing was complete. Locating a limit or a chart entry in the required publications without a reminder has not yet been asked of SP independently. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to locate one reference unprompted before doing so for the whole set of publications.
texts_at.1: SP used the Flight Manual, the Techniques and Procedures Manual, AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the aeronautical publications inside the standard required at this stage, the correct limit produced only after the IP indicated the chapter to open. The trend traces to study of the required publications being incomplete for this daily assignment. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to complete the study of every required publication for each assignment so references do not need to be indicated.
texts_at.2: SP used the required publications inside the standard required at this stage, one Flight Manual limit misstated at the pre-flight briefing because it was quoted from memory instead of the current publication. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to quote from the current publication rather than memory so the first statement is already correct.
texts_at.3: SP knew in detail the Flight Manual, the A/C Techniques and Procedures Manual, AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the aeronautical publications and used them with confidence throughout the navigation sortie, limits and procedures quoted correctly with the right reference, the small margin tracing to one MAIP entry being located a beat slower than the rest. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to hold the same location speed on every entry so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.1: SP used the Flight Manual, the Techniques and Procedures Manual, AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the aeronautical publications for the sortie, one reference located after a verbal reminder from the IP and the rest located unprompted. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the error without IP intervention, opened the manual and gave the correct value together with its paragraph within a few seconds, the remaining questions on the other publications answered accurately, after misstating a limit quoted from memory. Quoting from the current publication rather than memory from the start, rather than recognizing the error afterward, would remove even that correction. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound publication reference knowledge.
texts_above.3: SP knew in detail the Flight Manual, the A/C Techniques and Procedures Manual, AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the aeronautical publications and used them with confidence throughout the navigation sortie, limits, normal procedures, the applicable VFR rules and the route and airfield data quoted correctly with the right reference at both briefings. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sure-handed publication reference knowledge.
texts_above.4: SP used all handbooks related to the flight with complete confidence, quoting limits and procedures verbatim together with chapter and paragraph, and reading the route directly from the current chart and MAIP entries. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to exceptional publication reference knowledge.

error_modes.label: Knowledge of meteorological principles and attendance of the morning meteorological briefing

texts.0: SP, due to mission planning that did not address the forecast weather at the recovery time, could not interpret the wind, visibility and cloud information given at the morning meteorological briefing for the route. SP did not have knowledge of meteorological principles and could not follow the briefing without problem, and the IP had to explain the significance of the forecast for each leg. The visibility trend along the route was not identified at all and the sortie profile had to be reconstructed by the IP.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete preparation on meteorology, followed the morning meteorological briefing only in general terms and stated the effect of the forecast on the route only after the IP asked directed questions. Knowledge of meteorological principles stayed at the minimum acceptable limit and the implications for the en-route legs had to be drawn out verbally. SP finally identified the deteriorating visibility on the return leg, but only after being prompted twice.
texts.2: SP, due to a hurried reading of the forecast before the morning meteorological briefing, initially misjudged the significance of the wind change forecast for the middle leg of the route. SP re-examined the charts without IP intervention, corrected the assessment and stated the expected drift and the visibility trend before the crew briefing ended. The remaining meteorological information was interpreted correctly and used in the route plan.
texts.3: SP has knowledge of meteorological principles and attended the morning meteorological briefing without problem, interpreting the forecast wind, cloud and visibility for every leg of the route. SP stated the expected drift, the effect on leg times and the conditions expected at the recovery time accurately and without prompting. All meteorological questions at the post-flight briefing were answered correctly.
texts.4: SP interpreted the morning meteorological briefing with exceptional depth, explaining the mechanism behind the forecast conditions and the expected changes over the duration of the navigation sortie. SP linked the forecast to the specific legs of the route, stated the points where visibility could fall below VFR requirements and proposed the associated decision points before being asked. The assessment made during the briefing was confirmed by the actual conditions encountered.
texts.marginal: SP has the required knowledge of meteorological principles and followed the morning meteorological briefing without problem, but the interpretation stayed close to the printed forecast values without extending to their effect on the individual legs. The trend indicates that meteorological information is received correctly but is not yet fully converted into route planning. SP is expected to reach the point where every forecast element is translated directly into the expected conditions and timings of the navigation profile.

texts_at.0: With the IP explaining the significance of the forecast for each leg of the route, SP followed the explanation and needed it given for three legs during the morning meteorological briefing. Interpreting the forecast for a leg without a reminder has not yet been asked of SP at this stage. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to interpret one leg unprompted before doing so for the whole route.
texts_at.1: SP followed the morning meteorological briefing inside the standard required at this stage, the effect of the forecast on the route stated only after the IP asked directed questions. The trend traces to preparation on meteorology being incomplete before the briefing rather than covering every leg's implications. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to work through the implications for every leg before the briefing so the effect does not need to be drawn out with questions.
texts_at.2: SP followed the morning meteorological briefing inside the standard required at this stage, the significance of a wind change forecast for the middle leg initially misjudged from a hurried reading. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to read the full forecast without hurrying so the first assessment of each leg is already correct.
texts_at.3: SP has knowledge of meteorological principles and attended the morning meteorological briefing without problem, interpreting the forecast wind, cloud and visibility for every leg of the route, stating the expected drift and effect accurately, the small margin tracing to one implication being stated a beat after the rest of the leg's assessment. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to state every implication at the same point in the assessment so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.1: SP followed the morning meteorological briefing for the route, one leg interpreted after a verbal explanation from the IP and the rest interpreted unprompted. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP re-examined the charts without IP intervention, corrected the assessment and stated the expected drift and the visibility trend before the crew briefing ended, after initially misjudging the significance of a wind change forecast from a hurried reading. Reading the full forecast without hurrying from the start, rather than re-examining it after a misjudgment, would remove even that correction. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid meteorological interpretation.
texts_above.3: SP has knowledge of meteorological principles and attended the morning meteorological briefing without problem, interpreting the forecast wind, cloud and visibility for every leg of the route and stating the expected drift, the effect on leg times and the conditions expected at the recovery time accurately and without prompting. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to well-developed meteorological interpretation.
texts_above.4: SP interpreted the morning meteorological briefing with exceptional depth, explaining the mechanism behind the forecast conditions and the expected changes over the duration of the navigation sortie, linking the forecast to the specific legs of the route. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to outstanding meteorological interpretation.

error_modes.label: Aerodynamics knowledge and theoretical explanation of situations encountered in flight

texts.0: SP, due to not having studied the aerodynamics material supporting the navigation phase, could not explain theoretically the change in performance observed during the climb and the cruise legs of the sortie. SP does not have aerodynamics knowledge sufficient to explain situations to be encountered during flight, and gave contradictory answers on the relation between power, airspeed and fuel flow at cruise altitude. The IP had to teach the theoretical background at the post-flight briefing before the sortie could be debriefed.
texts.1: SP, due to superficial study of the theory, explained the aerodynamic behaviour observed on the route only in general terms and reached the correct explanation only after successive verbal indications from the IP. Aerodynamics knowledge remained at the minimum acceptable limit and the answers on cruise performance and on the effect of the turn on the ground track needed continuous guidance. The explanation was eventually complete, but it was produced by the IP's questions rather than by SP.
texts.2: SP, due to confusing two related concepts, first gave an incorrect theoretical explanation of the airspeed change observed during the climbing leg. SP recognized the inconsistency without IP intervention, reconsidered the reasoning and gave the correct explanation of the relation between power, weight and airspeed within the same answer. The remaining theoretical questions on the situations encountered during the navigation sortie were answered correctly.
texts.3: SP has aerodynamics knowledge and explained theoretically every situation encountered during the navigation sortie, including cruise performance, the effect of the turns on the ground track and the behaviour of the aircraft at the planned altitudes. The explanations were accurate, given without hesitation and correctly connected to what was actually observed in flight. No theoretical answer needed correction by the IP.
texts.4: SP explained the aerodynamics of the navigation profile at a level beyond that expected at this stage, connecting cruise performance, altitude selection and fuel flow into a single consistent picture. SP predicted before the flight how the aircraft would behave on each leg at the planned weight and altitude and confirmed the prediction against the actual figures at the post-flight briefing. Every theoretical question was answered with the correct reasoning and the correct reference.
texts.marginal: SP has the required aerodynamics knowledge and explained the situations encountered during flight to the acceptable standard, but the answers stayed at the level of definitions and did not always extend to the specific conditions of the sortie. The trend indicates that theory is retained but is not yet applied readily to what is observed on the route. SP is expected to link every theoretical concept directly to the performance seen during the navigation legs.

texts_at.0: With the IP teaching the theoretical background at the post-flight briefing, SP followed the explanation and needed two situations taught before the debrief could continue. Explaining a situation encountered in flight theoretically without a reminder has not yet been asked of SP independently. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to explain one situation unprompted before doing so for the whole sortie.
texts_at.1: SP explained the aerodynamics of the situations encountered on the route inside the standard required at this stage, the correct explanation on cruise performance reached only after successive verbal indications from the IP. The trend traces to study of the theory being superficial rather than connected to the specific behaviour observed on the route. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to connect the theory to the specific behaviour observed on each leg so the explanation does not need successive indications.
texts_at.2: SP explained the aerodynamics of the situations encountered on the route inside the standard required at this stage, an initial explanation of an airspeed change during the climbing leg confusing two related concepts before the correct one was given. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to separate those two concepts during preparation so the first explanation is already correct.
texts_at.3: SP has aerodynamics knowledge and explained theoretically every situation encountered during the navigation sortie, including cruise performance and the effect of the turns on the ground track, explanations accurate and connected to what was actually observed, the small margin tracing to one explanation being given a beat slower than the rest. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to hold the same explanation speed on every situation so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.1: SP explained the aerodynamics of the situations encountered on the route, one explanation following a verbal reminder from the IP and the rest given unprompted. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the inconsistency without IP intervention, reconsidered the reasoning and gave the correct explanation of the relation between power, weight and airspeed within the same answer, the remaining theoretical questions answered correctly, after initially confusing two related concepts on the climbing leg. Separating those two concepts during preparation from the start, rather than recognizing the inconsistency in the answer itself, would remove even that correction. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady aerodynamics knowledge application.
texts_above.3: SP has aerodynamics knowledge and explained theoretically every situation encountered during the navigation sortie, including cruise performance, the effect of the turns on the ground track and the behaviour of the aircraft at the planned altitudes, explanations accurate and given without hesitation. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to consistently accurate aerodynamics knowledge application.
texts_above.4: SP explained the aerodynamics of the navigation profile at a level beyond that expected at this stage, connecting cruise performance, altitude selection and fuel flow into a single consistent picture, predicting aircraft behaviour before the flight and confirming it afterward. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to exemplary aerodynamics knowledge application.

error_modes.label: Knowledge of airport traffic procedures and ability to plan a flight

texts.0: SP, due to lack of awareness of a published restriction that was available in the briefing material, could not state the traffic procedures of the en-route and alternate airfields used in the navigation plan. SP does not know airport traffic procedures and does not have sufficient knowledge in order to plan a flight, and the route, the fuel figures and the alternate selection had to be produced by the IP. The flight plan presented at the pre-flight briefing was not usable and was rewritten before departure.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete study of the airfield data, presented a flight plan in which the entry procedure for the en-route airfield and the fuel reserve were corrected only after successive verbal indications from the IP. Knowledge of airport traffic procedures remained at the minimum acceptable limit and each element of the plan had to be checked verbally before it was accepted. The plan was finally correct, but the corrections delayed the briefing and were not initiated by SP.
texts.2: SP, due to using an outdated note instead of the current publication, initially planned the arrival at the en-route airfield with the wrong pattern direction. SP identified the discrepancy without IP intervention, checked the current MAIP entry and corrected the arrival procedure and the associated timing before the plan was presented. The rest of the flight plan, including the alternate and the fuel figures, was complete and correct.
texts.3: SP knows airport traffic procedures and has sufficient knowledge in order to plan a flight, and presented a complete navigation plan with correct route, timings, fuel figures, alternate and airfield entry and exit procedures. All questions on the traffic procedures of the departure, en-route and alternate airfields were answered accurately and without prompting. The plan was accepted at the pre-flight briefing without correction.
texts.4: SP planned the navigation sortie to a standard above that expected at this stage, presenting the route with alternative options for the alternate airfield and the associated fuel and timing consequences of each one. SP quoted the traffic procedures of every airfield on the route together with the applicable restrictions and their source, and identified in advance the points where a change of plan would be required. The plan needed no correction and was used as briefed.
texts.marginal: SP knows airport traffic procedures and planned the flight to the required standard, but the planning of the alternate and of the en-route diversion options was noticeably less developed than the planning of the primary route. The trend indicates that preparation is concentrated on the intended profile rather than on its alternatives. SP is expected to plan the alternate and diversion options with the same completeness as the primary route.

texts_at.0: With the IP producing the route, the fuel figures and the alternate selection for the flight plan, SP followed the plan read back and needed two elements produced before the plan was usable. Presenting a usable flight plan without a reminder has not yet been asked of SP independently. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to produce one element of the plan unprompted before doing so for the whole plan.
texts_at.1: SP planned the navigation flight inside the standard required at this stage, the entry procedure for the en-route airfield and the fuel reserve corrected only after successive verbal indications from the IP. The trend traces to study of the airfield data being incomplete rather than checked against the current publication. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to check every airfield entry against the current publication so corrections are not needed at the briefing.
texts_at.2: SP planned the navigation flight inside the standard required at this stage, the arrival at the en-route airfield initially planned with the wrong pattern direction because an outdated note was used instead of the current publication. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to plan directly from the current publication rather than a note so the first plan is already correct.
texts_at.3: SP knows airport traffic procedures and has sufficient knowledge in order to plan a flight, presenting a complete navigation plan with correct route, timings, fuel figures, alternate and airfield entry and exit procedures, the small margin tracing to one procedure being confirmed a beat after the plan was presented rather than before it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to confirm every procedure before presenting the plan so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.1: SP planned the navigation flight, one element of the plan produced after a verbal reminder from the IP and the rest produced unprompted. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP identified the discrepancy without IP intervention, checked the current MAIP entry and corrected the arrival procedure and the associated timing before the plan was presented, the rest of the flight plan complete and correct, after an outdated note had produced the wrong pattern direction. Planning directly from the current publication from the start, rather than identifying the discrepancy afterward, would remove even that correction. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable flight planning knowledge.
texts_above.3: SP knows airport traffic procedures and has sufficient knowledge in order to plan a flight, presenting a complete navigation plan with correct route, timings, fuel figures, alternate and airfield entry and exit procedures, all questions answered accurately and without prompting. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to notably good flight planning knowledge.
texts_above.4: SP planned the navigation sortie to a standard above that expected at this stage, presenting the route with alternative options for the alternate airfield and the associated fuel and timing consequences of each one. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to superior flight planning knowledge.

error_modes.label: Knowledge of air medicine and flight physiology, and interpretation of physiological conditions and flight effects

texts.0: SP, due to not having studied the air medicine material of the phase, could not interpret the physiological conditions and flight effects associated with the altitudes and the duration of the navigation sortie. SP does not have knowledge of air medicine and flight physiology and gave incorrect answers on the recognition and the immediate actions for hypoxia and for the visual illusions expected over featureless terrain. The IP had to teach the recognition criteria and the corrective actions before the sortie could be debriefed.
texts.1: SP, due to superficial study of flight physiology, described the physiological effects expected on the route only in general terms and gave the recognition signs and the required actions only after directed questions from the IP. Knowledge of air medicine remained at the minimum acceptable limit and the connection between the planned altitudes, the sortie duration and the expected effects had to be drawn out verbally. The answers were finally correct, but they were reached with continuous guidance.
texts.2: SP, due to confusing the symptoms of two related conditions, first gave an incomplete description of the effects expected during the higher legs of the navigation profile. SP corrected the answer without IP intervention, separated the two conditions and stated the recognition signs and the required actions for each one accurately. The remaining questions on flight physiology and on the effects of the sortie duration were answered correctly.
texts.3: SP has knowledge of air medicine and flight physiology and interpreted correctly all the physiological conditions and flight effects to be encountered on the navigation sortie. SP stated the recognition signs, the immediate actions and the preventive measures for the altitudes, the duration and the visual environment of the route without prompting. All questions at the post-flight briefing were answered accurately.
texts.4: SP interpreted the physiological aspects of the navigation profile at a level beyond that expected at this stage, connecting altitude, sortie duration, hydration and visual environment into a single assessment of personal fitness for the flight. SP described the recognition signs and the required actions for each expected effect and stated in advance the points of the route where the risk would be highest. Every answer was accurate and supported by the correct reference.
texts.marginal: SP has the required knowledge of air medicine and flight physiology and interpreted the expected conditions to the acceptable standard, but the answers on the visual illusions associated with long legs over uniform terrain were less complete than the rest. The trend indicates that the physiological material is known in general but not yet applied fully to the specific environment of navigation flying. SP is expected to cover the visual and fatigue related effects of this category with the same depth as the remaining physiology material.

texts_at.0: With the IP teaching the recognition criteria and the corrective actions for the physiological conditions expected on the route, SP followed the explanation and needed two conditions taught before the debrief could continue. Interpreting a physiological condition without a reminder has not yet been asked of SP independently. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to interpret one condition unprompted before doing so for the whole sortie.
texts_at.1: SP interpreted the physiological conditions and flight effects of the sortie inside the standard required at this stage, the recognition signs and required actions for hypoxia given only after directed questions from the IP. The trend traces to study of flight physiology being superficial rather than connected to the planned altitudes and duration. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to connect the physiology study to the planned altitudes and duration so recognition signs do not need directed questions.
texts_at.2: SP interpreted the physiological conditions and flight effects of the sortie inside the standard required at this stage, an initial description of the effects during the higher legs incomplete because two related conditions were confused. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to separate those two conditions during preparation so the first description is already complete.
texts_at.3: SP has knowledge of air medicine and flight physiology and interpreted correctly all the physiological conditions and flight effects to be encountered on the navigation sortie, recognition signs, immediate actions and preventive measures stated without prompting, the small margin tracing to one answer being given a beat slower than the rest. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to hold the same recall speed on every answer so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.2: SP corrected the answer without IP intervention, separated the two conditions and stated the recognition signs and the required actions for each one accurately, the remaining questions on flight physiology answered correctly, after initially confusing two related conditions for the higher legs. Separating those two conditions during preparation from the start, rather than correcting the answer afterward, would remove even that correction. error_modes.label: Awareness of sea and land survival procedures and of rescue procedures from SAR means

texts.0: SP, due to not having reviewed the survival material before the navigation sortie, could not state the sea and land survival procedures applicable to the terrain and the sea sectors crossed by the planned route. SP is not aware of the rescue procedures from SAR means and could not describe the use of the survival equipment carried or the actions expected after an ejection over the route. The IP had to present the survival and SAR procedures in full before the sortie could be briefed.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete study of the survival procedures, described the actions after a forced landing or ejection along the route only in outline and completed them only after successive verbal indications from the IP. texts_above.2: SP identified the drift without IP input, returned to A/C control, restored the profile and then performed the second FEVER check to verify the boldface effect, each following checklist closed with a return to A/C control, after the profile had drifted for a few seconds during a PCL movement below 60 percent. Compensating with control stick, rudder and PCL whenever the PCL moves below 60 percent from the start, rather than identifying the drift afterward, would remove even that excursion. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable boldface verification technique.
texts_above.3: SP stated the boldface steps before executing them and confirmed after each one that the A/C was still under control, the effect of every boldface verified with a further FEVER check, asking in turn whether another boldface applied and continuing the loop until none remained. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to notably good boldface verification technique.
texts_above.4: SP worked the boldface loop faultlessly, stating the steps, executing them, re-checking A/C control and verifying the effect with a further FEVER check on each pass, identifying without prompting that the engine failure during flight case could lead to the immediate engine start boldface. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to superior boldface verification technique.

error_modes.label: Declare with a plan: nature of the emergency, time to landing, souls on board and briefing to ATC
error_modes.source: technique:1.21 TABLETOP AND STAND-UP EMERGENCY PROCEDURES (EPS)

texts.0: SP, due to declaring the emergency before a game plan had been established, transmitted only that a problem existed and could not state to ATC the nature of the emergency, the time to landing, the souls on board or the plan of action. SP had not decided the pattern to be flown or how the A/C would be stopped on the ground. The IP had to establish the plan and make the transmission before the practice could continue.
texts.1: SP declared the emergency with a plan, but produced the four items of the report to ATC only after repeated verbal prompting, and the time to landing was given as an estimate without reference to the position on the route. The intended pattern was named, yet the method of stopping the A/C was stated only after the IP asked. Communication stayed at the minimum acceptable limit and the transmission had to be repeated in the correct order.
texts.2: SP, due to transmitting before the plan was complete, omitted the souls on board on the first call to ATC. SP recognized the omission without IP input and passed the missing item together with the intended pattern in the following transmission a few seconds later. The rest of the report contained the nature of the emergency, the time to landing and the plan of action, correctly ordered.
texts.3: SP established the game plan first and then declared the emergency, giving ATC the nature of the emergency, the time to landing, the souls on board and the briefing of the intended action. The pattern type was named and SP stated how the A/C would be stopped, on the runway with emergency ground egress, on a taxiway or taxied back to parking. No item of the report had to be prompted.
texts.4: SP declared the emergency with a complete plan and delivered the four report items to ATC in one concise transmission, with the time to landing derived from the actual position on the route and the fuel remaining. SP also stated the alternate plan should the nearest suitable airfield become unusable and the local NORDO procedure found in the in-flight guide. The appropriate authorities were informed in the correct order and without any prompting.
texts.marginal: SP declared the emergency with a plan and passed all four items to ATC, but the briefing of the plan of action was given in general terms and the time to landing was rounded without reference to the leg being flown. The transmission was acceptable on this scenario, yet the trend shows the report learned as a list rather than derived from the plan. SP is expected to state the nature of the emergency, time to landing, souls on board and plan of action as consequences of the game plan already established.

texts_at.0: With the IP establishing the plan and making the transmission to ATC, SP followed the declaration read back and needed the plan established before the practice could continue. Declaring an emergency with a complete plan without a reminder has not yet been asked of SP independently. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to state one element of the plan unprompted before declaring the whole emergency independently.
texts_at.1: SP declared the emergency with a plan inside the standard required at this stage, the four items of the ATC report produced only after repeated verbal prompting. The trend traces to the time to landing being given as an estimate rather than derived from position on the route. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to derive the time to landing from position on the route so it does not read as an estimate.
texts_at.2: SP declared the emergency with a plan inside the standard required at this stage, souls on board omitted from the first call to ATC before the plan was made complete. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to check the four report items against a fixed list before the first transmission so none is omitted.
texts_at.3: SP established the game plan first and then declared the emergency, giving ATC the nature of the emergency, the time to landing, the souls on board and the briefing of the intended action, the pattern type named, the small margin tracing to the method of stopping the A/C being stated a beat after the pattern type rather than with it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to state the stopping method together with the pattern type so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.1: SP declared the emergency with a plan, one element of the plan following a verbal reminder from the IP and the rest declared unprompted. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the omission without IP input and passed the missing item together with the intended pattern in the following transmission a few seconds later, the rest of the report correctly ordered, after souls on board had been omitted from the first call to ATC. Checking the four report items against a fixed list before the first transmission, rather than recognizing the omission afterward, would remove even that second call. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured emergency declaration content.
texts_above.3: SP established the game plan first and then declared the emergency, giving ATC the nature of the emergency, the time to landing, the souls on board and the briefing of the intended action, the pattern type named and the method of stopping the A/C stated. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to precise emergency declaration content.
texts_above.4: SP declared the emergency with a complete plan and delivered the four report items to ATC in one concise transmission, the time to landing derived from the actual position on the route and the fuel remaining, an alternate plan also stated in advance. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to first-rate emergency declaration content.

error_modes.label: Formation terminology on the navigation sortie: HCA and angle off, aspect angle, the 3/9 line and the meaning of stabilize
error_modes.source: technique:9.17 TERMINOLOGY - HCA, ASPECT ANGLE, PURSUIT, LOS, TURN CIRCLE

texts.0: SP, due to not having studied the formation terminology applicable to the navigation sorties flown in formation, used aspect angle as a clock position and could not define heading crossing angle or state that it is synonymous with angle off. SP did not know the meaning of the 3/9 line and answered that stabilize means stop. The IP had to teach the terminology of the section before the formation part of the navigation profile could be briefed.
texts.1: SP defined heading crossing angle and aspect angle only in outline and expressed aspect in clock positions until corrected verbally by the IP. The requirement for Number 2 to remain aft of the 3/9 line of Number 1 during manoeuvres was stated only after prompting. Knowledge of the terminology stayed at the minimum acceptable limit and every definition had to be completed by the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to confusing the two terms during the briefing, described the lag pursuit picture with the values that belong to lead pursuit. SP recognized the error without IP input, restated that on lag pursuit aspect decreases and heading crossing angle increases while closure decreases, and gave aspect correctly in degrees off the tail in multiples of 10. The remaining terminology questions were answered accurately.
texts.3: SP knew the formation terminology used on the navigation sorties and defined heading crossing angle, angle off, aspect angle, line of sight and line of sight rate correctly. Aspect was expressed in degrees off the tail and not as a clock position, the 3/9 line was identified as the 90 degrees aspect line and stabilize was explained as under control and not as stop. No definition required correction by the IP.
texts.4: SP used the formation terminology with complete confidence, describing the lead, pure and lag pursuit pictures with the corresponding aspect, line of sight and closure behaviour. SP quoted the T-6 turn circle radius of approximately 8000 feet and the turn rate of approximately 3 degrees per second at 10000 feet MSL, 30 degrees bank and 180 KIAS, and explained how turning room is used aft of the 3/9 line. Every answer was linked correctly to the manoeuvres of the formation navigation profile.
texts.marginal: SP knew the formation terminology to the required standard, but the answers on aspect angle and line of sight rate were slower and less precise than those on heading crossing angle. Definitions were correct, yet aspect was twice about to be expressed as a clock position before SP corrected the wording. SP is expected to consolidate the terminology so that aspect, line of sight and pursuit pictures are described with the same precision as angle off.

texts_at.0: With the IP teaching the terminology of the section at the briefing table, SP followed the definitions read back and needed two terms taught before the formation part of the profile could be briefed. Defining a formation term without a reminder has not yet been asked of SP independently. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to define one term unprompted before doing so for the whole terminology set.
texts_at.1: SP defined heading crossing angle, aspect angle and the 3/9 line inside the standard required at this stage, the requirement for Number 2 to remain aft of the 3/9 line stated only after prompting. The trend traces to the definitions being given in outline rather than to the level of a stated distinguishing example. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to prepare a distinguishing example for every definition so it does not need to be prompted.
texts_at.2: SP defined heading crossing angle, aspect angle and the 3/9 line inside the standard required at this stage, the lag pursuit picture initially described with lead pursuit values before the two terms were confused and then separated. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to rehearse lead and lag pursuit side by side so the two are not confused.
texts_at.3: SP knew the formation terminology used on the navigation sorties and defined heading crossing angle, angle off, aspect angle, line of sight and line of sight rate correctly, aspect expressed in degrees off the tail and not as a clock position, the small margin tracing to one definition being given a beat slower than the rest. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to hold the same recall speed on every definition so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.1: SP defined the formation terminology of the section, one term following a verbal reminder from the IP and the rest defined unprompted. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the error without IP input, restated that on lag pursuit aspect decreases and heading crossing angle increases while closure decreases, and gave aspect correctly in degrees off the tail in multiples of 10, the remaining terminology questions answered accurately, after initially confusing the two pursuit pictures. Rehearsing lead and lag pursuit side by side from the start, rather than recognizing the confusion during the answer, would remove even that correction. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent formation terminology knowledge.
texts_above.3: SP knew the formation terminology used on the navigation sorties and defined heading crossing angle, angle off, aspect angle, line of sight and line of sight rate correctly, aspect expressed in degrees off the tail, the 3/9 line identified as the 90 degrees aspect line and stabilize explained as under control rather than stop. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to disciplined formation terminology knowledge.
texts_above.4: SP used the formation terminology with complete confidence, describing the lead, pure and lag pursuit pictures with the corresponding aspect, line of sight and closure behaviour, quoting the T-6 turn circle radius and turn rate precisely. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to faultless formation terminology knowledge.

error_modes.label: Range estimation by mil-sizing using the AOA indexer, the mirrors and the wingtip strobe flash guard

texts.0: SP, due to not knowing the mil-sizing method, could not state that one mil equals one foot at 1000 feet and could not name a single cockpit reference used to compare the size of the other A/C. SP gave no apparent size for the T-6 at 300, 500 or 1000 feet and did not associate the detail cues, such as the readable tail flash or the loss of A/C detail, with any range. The IP had to teach the range estimation table before the formation part of the navigation sortie could be briefed.
texts.1: SP stated the mil definition but produced the apparent sizes of the T-6 at the three reference ranges only after repeated verbal prompting, and named only the mirrors as a comparison reference. The AOA indexer and the wingtip anti-collision strobe flash guard were recalled after the IP mentioned them. Knowledge of range estimation stayed at the minimum acceptable limit and the detail cues were listed by the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to recalling the table from memory instead of the cockpit references, gave the 500 feet cue as one quarter of the mirror width instead of one half. SP identified the error without IP input and restated the set correctly, with approximately 111 mils at 300 feet, 67 mils at 500 feet and 33 mils at 1000 feet, all measured at 20 inches from the eye. The remaining range estimation questions were answered accurately.
texts.3: SP knew the mil-sizing method and stated that one mil equals one foot at 1000 feet, giving the T-6 apparent sizes of approximately 111, 67 and 33 mils at 300, 500 and 1000 feet. The comparison references were named correctly as the AOA indexer, the canopy bow mirrors and the wingtip anti-collision strobe flash guard, together with the detail cues for each range. The method was then applied consistently in flight without prompting.
texts.4: SP explained the mil-sizing method in exceptional detail, including the measurement at 20 inches from the pilot's eye and the reason why the same table is valid regardless of the position of the other A/C. Each reference range was supported by both a size comparison and a detail cue, from readable tail flash letters at 300 feet to the loss of A/C detail at 1000 feet. SP cross-checked the estimated ranges in flight against the visual cues and reported them accurately throughout the navigation profile.
texts.marginal: SP knew the range estimation method to the required standard, but recalled the size comparisons faster than the detail cues and hesitated on the 500 feet references. The estimates given in flight were acceptable, yet the trend shows reliance on a single cockpit reference. SP is expected to use the AOA indexer, the mirrors and the wingtip strobe flash guard together with the detail cues so that range estimation stays reliable when one reference is not usable.

texts_at.0: With the IP teaching the range estimation table at the briefing table, SP followed the table read back and needed it taught before the formation part of the sortie could be briefed. Stating an apparent size or a comparison reference from the mil-sizing method without a reminder has not yet been asked of SP independently. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to state one reference range unprompted before doing so for the whole table.
texts_at.1: SP applied the mil-sizing method inside the standard required at this stage, the apparent sizes of the T-6 at the three reference ranges produced only after repeated verbal prompting. The trend traces to only the mirrors being named as a comparison reference rather than all three cockpit references. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to name all three cockpit references from the start so recall does not need prompting.
texts_at.2: SP applied the mil-sizing method inside the standard required at this stage, the 500 feet cue given as one quarter of the mirror width instead of one half before the error was identified. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to check each reference range against the printed table so the first statement of a cue is already correct.
texts_at.3: SP knew the mil-sizing method and stated that one mil equals one foot at 1000 feet, giving the T-6 apparent sizes of approximately 111, 67 and 33 mils at 300, 500 and 1000 feet, comparison references named correctly, the small margin tracing to one detail cue being recalled a beat slower than the rest. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to hold the same recall speed on every detail cue so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.1: SP applied the mil-sizing method for range estimation, one reference range following a verbal reminder from the IP and the rest stated unprompted. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP identified the error without IP input and restated the set correctly, with approximately 111 mils at 300 feet, 67 mils at 500 feet and 33 mils at 1000 feet, all measured at 20 inches from the eye, the remaining range estimation questions answered accurately, after giving the 500 feet cue incorrectly from memory. Checking each reference range against the printed table from the start, rather than identifying the error afterward, would remove even that correction. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good range estimation technique.
texts_above.3: SP knew the mil-sizing method and stated that one mil equals one foot at 1000 feet, giving the T-6 apparent sizes of approximately 111, 67 and 33 mils at 300, 500 and 1000 feet, the comparison references named correctly together with the detail cues for each range. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to very good range estimation technique.
texts_above.4: SP explained the mil-sizing method in exceptional detail, including the measurement at 20 inches from the pilot's eye and the reason why the same table is valid regardless of the position of the other A/C. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to excellent range estimation technique.
